drug_class: Antidepressant / Smoking Cessation Aid (NDRI - Norepinephrine-Dopamine Reuptake Inhibitor)
purpose: Bupropion is mainly used to treat depression and seasonal affective disorder (SAD), which is a type of depression that comes with the change of seasons. It is also prescribed to help people quit smoking. Sometimes doctors use it to help with attention and focus as well.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical messengers called dopamine and norepinephrine to help regulate your mood, energy, and motivation. Bupropion works by keeping more of these chemicals available in your brain for longer. Unlike many other antidepressants, it does not affect serotonin, which means it tends to have fewer sexual side effects.
common_side_effects: Dry mouth, headache, trouble sleeping or insomnia, nausea, dizziness, constipation, increased sweating, and feeling jittery or anxious. Many of these side effects are mild and often improve after the first couple of weeks as your body adjusts.
warnings: Bupropion can lower your seizure threshold, meaning it can increase your risk of having a seizure — especially at higher doses. Do NOT take it if you have a history of seizures or an eating disorder like bulimia or anorexia. It should not be taken with an MAO inhibitor. Like all antidepressants, it may increase thoughts of suicide in some young people, especially early in treatment — contact your doctor right away if this happens. Avoid alcohol. Tell your doctor about all medications you take.
typical_dosing: For depression, the starting dose is usually 100–150 mg once or twice a day, and your doctor may slowly increase it to 300–450 mg per day depending on the form prescribed. For quitting smoking (Zyban), you typically start at 150 mg once daily for 3 days, then increase to 150 mg twice daily for 7–12 weeks. Always take it exactly as your doctor tells you, and never crush or chew the extended-release tablets.
